features.headline: Perfect 2026-27 MLB free agency moves for teams to watch
features.desc: Who most needs an ace? Which contender should make a blockbuster trade? Jeff Passan digs in.
body: LAS VEGAS — The sense of urgency across Major League Baseball right now is palpable. Everyone in the industry knows the game is shutting down when the clock strikes midnight on Dec.
2 and the owners lock the players out, and the transaction freeze that accompanies it makes the next three weeks that much more important.

In the final days before the last lockout in 2021, teams guaranteed more than $1.5 billion to free agents. This week at baseball's GM meetings, executives and agents are anticipating a similar deluge of deals as November progresses.

The parties have skipped the standard early-winter formalities and gone straight to expressions of interest. And with the shortened timetable, offers are expected to follow soon — especially following next week's owners' meetings.

The unknown labor situation's impact has been front and center on the minds of executives and agents here. Some believe owners see an opportunity to exert pressure on a large group of players and squeeze.
Others think teams will spend like any other year to ensure players, in a potential legal battle, cannot suggest any sort of collusive behavior.

It's not a bonanza free agent class by any means, but after an October in which three small-market organizations were among the four playing in league championship series, teams regard the current landscape as wide open enough that few plan to punt on the 2027 season.
With that in mind, here is the perfect offseason move for the dozen returning playoff teams and five others expected to be active during the shortened transaction window.

features.headline: Tarik Skubal free agency tracker: Latest on top MLB free agent
features.desc: Who will land the two-time Cy Young Award winner? We have all the latest updates on where things stand.
body: All eyes are on ace Tarik Skubal as MLB free agency gets underway ahead of the impending labor stoppage.

The current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, meaning that after that, no players can sign until a new CBA is established. This could put Skubal on the fast track to a new contract, as many around the sport expect him to sign ahead of the lockout.
Where do things currently stand in Skubal's free agency? What's the latest? We have everything you need to know about the winter's No. 1 free agent in one place.
Skubal is scheduled to meet with the New York Mets in California next week, a source confirmed to ESPN on Tuesday.

While the Mets are an obvious possible landing spot for the two-time Cy Young Award winner, the other seemingly logical destination for Skubal is a return to the Los Angeles Dodgers, the team he was traded to from the Detroit Tigers at this year's deadline.

Nov. 11: Passan's perfect move for top contenders: Skubal has no interest in a shorter-term, higher-dollar deal, which could disadvantage the Dodgers. The Mets could be in the strongest position to land Skubal this offseason.
Nov. 10: Mets to meet with prized ace Skubal next week: The Mets have a need for front-line starting pitching and an owner in Steve Cohen who's willing to spend.
Nov. 3: Rankings, contract projections for top 50 MLB free agents: Skubal comes in as the top-ranked free agent of this offseason — but what will his contract look like?
Nov. 2: MLB offseason rumors and intel: What we're hearing as free agency begins: Outside of the Dodgers and Mets, the Cubs and San Diego Padres are other teams with a rotation need.

features.headline: Questions on 2026 NFL trade deadline deals: Does Kirk Cousins lift the Vikings?
features.desc: Let's make sense of Kirk Cousins to the Vikings, Josh Downs to the Chiefs, the Jaguars getting aggressive, a wild Bengals comp-pick mixup and four teams' deadline silence.
body: For all the big names rumored to be in the mix Tuesday afternoon, the most significant trade of the day involved Titans safety Amani Hooker, who was dealt to the Bills with a fifth-round pick for a second-round selection.

The Vikings reunited with quarterback Kirk Cousins for a third-round selection, but the biggest moves ended up taking place Monday, when the Jaguars sent out a first-round pick and two second-round selections to land Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III.
What we saw over the past 24 hours left me with more questions than answers. So, I set out to try to answer those questions.

I'll get to the Cousins deal, a trade that was ruined by the internet and the teams that missed an opportunity to make a deal, but I have to start this in Florida, where a Jags regime that has been very happy to bet on themselves doubled down.

Jump to: Did the Jaguars give up too much? Can Cousins elevate the Vikings enough? What happened with the Bengals? What does Downs mean for the Chiefs? Why weren't there more trades? Which teams missed out?

The most fascinating team at the deadline did its work Monday with a series of stunning trades. The impetus for those moves, seemingly, goes back to a pair of relatively under-the-radar injuries in the Week 8 win over the Colts.
During that game, defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton tore his quadriceps muscle, and safety Eric Murray injured his elbow. Both are expected to sit out the rest of the season.

Hamilton and Murray aren't bad players — Hamilton was having his best season as a pro — but they're not the sort of load-bearing, cornerstone contributors who would lead a front office to panic that the defense will collapse without them.

features.headline: Facts vs. Feelings: Seven starts, streams and stashes for Week 10 and beyond
features.desc: Whether you feel like streaming Aaron Rodgers or stashing Jordyn Tyson, Liz Loza has the facts to support the case.
body: It was a passing comment delivered by one of my favorite editors. (Hi, Keith.) We were wrapping up a weekly content meeting and he was referencing the nearly barren trees, almost apologizing on behalf of the leaves.
How dare they not cling to their branches until after I've left the state? I appreciated his thoughtfulness, a gentle nod to L.A.'s endless summer and my own quiet craving for autumn's golden kitsch.

A small gesture that made a surprisingly big impact. It's been rolling around my brain all afternoon. Because he's right. The temps are dropping. The sun is setting at a disrespectful hour. And the year is in its final act. Now begins the long goodbye.

It's not all maudlin, of course. There's plenty to look forward to: family gatherings, pie, twinkle lights and more pie. Despite the veneer of cheer, however, the closing of any chapter forces reflection... whether we're ready for it or not.

The reckoning isn't here yet. But we can hear the whisper. That's the tough part. Because while there still exists time for change, we're also aware of the shrinking opportunity share. Do we throw in the towel and look to next year?
Or double down to salvage the back half? Maybe we surprise everyone and pivot, just for the sake of the plot. Regardless of the avenue chosen, a choice must be made.

The Cardinals — with their magic evaporating — appear to have chosen Option A. The Texans — resolute to shake off a disastrous 0-4 start — appear to have opted for Option B. The Browns — a squad that hasn't managed five wins over nine games since 2023 — regularly seem in play for Option C. What Big Brass decides is, ultimately, out of our control.

features.headline: How Harry Kane rose to win Ballon d'Or and became an England legend
features.desc: Harry Kane went from overlooked youngster to Ballon d'Or winner. Now he's about to become England's record appearance-holder — and possibly their greatest-ever player.
body: Another week, another landmark moment for Harry Kane. Life is like that right now for the England captain, who will become his country's all-time record appearance-maker when leading out the Three Lions against Croatia on Thursday.

It completes a remarkable fortnight for Kane, 33, after he won the men's Ballon d'Or for the first time and signed a new contract with Bayern Munich through to 2029. He is now one of the highest-paid players in Europe, at more than €30 million per year.

Surpassing Peter Shilton's 125-cap England record felt almost impossible for more than three decades, especially for an outfield player. Wayne Rooney reached 120, David Beckham 115, Steven Gerrard 114 and Ashley Cole 107, but Kane will go clear on his own with years still ahead of him.

- Kane's long road to Ballon d'Or glory ends with crowning moment - USMNT or Manchester United: Pros and cons of Pochettino's options - Why Messi won't be 'do a Wrexham' as owner of non-league Cornellà

England's goal-scoring record appeared a similarly difficult climb. Sir Bobby Charlton's tally of 49 stood for 45 years before Rooney reached the half-century in 2015 and later ended on 53. Kane is on a remarkable 91 — and counting.

He has captained England more often than any other player in history, leading England to back-to-back European Championship finals and a third-place finish at this summer's World Cup, the men's national team's best placing since their sole 1966 triumph.

The only thing missing is a major international trophy, something he willingly admits he would trade every individual accolade to have. But Kane's case for becoming England's greatest-ever player grows with each passing season.

features.headline: How a 24-hour trip across America showcased what makes college hoops special
features.desc: Every marathon has a beginning — and an end. We got to college hoops' heart over 24 incredible hours.
body: ROCK HILL, S.C. — Isaiah Howard saw his chance and took it.

With 7:17 left in the first half of a Nov. 2 game against Northern Illinois, the Grambling State guard took a pass from teammate Brandon Hardy and took flight for a transition dunk. He soared past Huskies defender Bennett Basich and thundered the ball through the hoop.
Fans behind the hoop jumped to their feet. The Rock Hill Sports & Event Center rocked. As Howard flexed in celebration, the local time flashed on the clock.
In August, college basketball media network Field of 68 announced it would resurrect a college basketball opening-day marathon.
Originally put on by ESPN, from 2008 to 2017, the event featured 24 hours of college basketball starting the moment the clock struck midnight on the chosen day.
The tradition ended after 2017, until Field of 68 brought it back in 2025, albeit in a more limited format — hosting games all day, starting at 8 a.m. ET.
This time, they went full tilt: four cascading tipoffs in Rock Hill, South Carolina, starting at midnight, then in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, followed by games in Rock Hill at night.
If this was a marathon, it would need a runner.
The pitch to my boss: Send me to the games in South Carolina and let me document the ensuing all-nighter.

Let me see what happens when sport spotlights its smaller programs, even if that spotlight is at 3 a.m. Let me sit beside the sport's most hard-core, intense fans. Let me bear witness to college basketball's land of early and equal opportunity.
